title: FLATTEN and LATERAL for nested data
objective: Explode JSON arrays into one row per element (json_each ≈ LATERAL FLATTEN), keep parents with empty arrays (OUTER), avoid fan-out when flattening two arrays, and reconcile flattened data with relational tables.
context: Finance doesn't trust the new event pipeline yet. Before order_items is rebuilt from the raw feed, they want proof: line-level data flattened from JSON must tie out to the existing order_items, and the new tags must be reportable.

exercises.title: One row per JSON order line
exercises.question: Finance wants to see the raw line data for the first five orders.
exercises.prompt: Flatten $.items for events whose $.order_id is between 1 and 5 and return order_id, line_no (the 0-based array position), product_id, qty and price (from each item).
hints: FROM raw_order_events e, json_each(e.payload, '$.items') i — one row per item.
i.key is the position; i.value is the item object, so read fields with i.value ->> '$.qty'.

SELECT e.payload ->> '$.order_id' AS order_id, i.key AS line_no, i.value ->> '$.product_id' AS product_id, i.value ->> '$.qty' AS qty, i.value ->> '$.price' AS price FROM raw_order_events e, json_each(e.payload,'$.items') i WHERE ...
exercises.why: This is the core transformation from event-shaped to table-shaped data.

recall.q: Which column of json_each holds the array position?

exercises.snowflake: SELECT e.payload:order_id::INT AS order_id, i.index AS line_no, i.value:product_id::INT AS product_id, i.value:qty::INT AS qty, i.value:price::NUMBER(10,2) AS price FROM raw_order_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:items) i WHERE e.payload:order_id::INT BETWEEN 1 AND 5;

exercises.title: Tag frequency
exercises.question: Marketing: how many orders carry each tag?
exercises.prompt: Flatten $.tags and return tag and tagged_events (number of events carrying that tag).
hints: Tags are plain strings, so the element itself (t.value) is the tag.
Events without a tags key produce no rows from json_each — fine here.
SELECT t.value AS tag, COUNT(*) AS tagged_events FROM raw_order_events e, json_each(e.payload,'$.tags') t GROUP BY t.value;
exercises.why: Multi-valued attributes (tags, categories, experiments) can't be grouped until flattened.

recall.q: Why don't untagged events appear in an inner flatten?
recall.a: json_each/FLATTEN of a missing or empty array yields zero rows, so the parent row disappears.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT t.value::STRING AS tag, COUNT(*) AS tagged_events FROM raw_order_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:tags) t GROUP BY 1;

exercises.title: Keep untagged orders (OUTER flatten)
exercises.question: Customer 7's account manager wants every one of their order events with its tags — untagged orders must still appear.
exercises.prompt: For events whose $.customer.id is 7, return order_id and tag: one row per tag, and exactly one row with tag NULL for events that have no tags.
hints: An inner flatten drops events without tags. You need the OUTER behaviour.
In SQLite: LEFT JOIN json_each(e.payload, '$.tags') AS t ON 1 = 1.
SELECT e.payload ->> '$.order_id' AS order_id, t.value AS tag FROM raw_order_events e LEFT JOIN json_each(e.payload,'$.tags') t ON 1 = 1 WHERE e.payload ->> '$.customer.id' = 7;
exercises.why: Forgetting OUTER => TRUE is the FLATTEN equivalent of using INNER JOIN when you meant LEFT JOIN.

recall.q: Snowflake option that keeps rows whose array is empty or missing?

exercises.snowflake: SELECT e.payload:order_id::INT AS order_id, t.value::STRING AS tag FROM raw_order_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:tags, OUTER => TRUE) t WHERE e.payload:customer.id::INT = 7;

exercises.title: Units by category from JSON lines
exercises.question: Merchandising wants units sold per category straight from the event feed.
exercises.prompt: Flatten $.items, keep only valid orders (join orders on order_id; order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), join products on the item's product_id, and return category (NULL shown as 'Uncategorized') and units (sum of qty).
hints: Flattened fields join to tables like normal columns.
Two joins: orders on the payload order_id (for status), products on i.value ->> '$.product_id'.

... FROM raw_order_events e JOIN json_each(e.payload,'$.items') i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = e.payload ->> '$.order_id' JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.value ->> '$.product_id' WHERE o.order_status IN (...) GROUP BY 1;
exercises.why: Once flattened, JSON lines behave like any fact table — and should produce the same numbers as the modelled tables (next exercises prove it).

recall.q: Can json_each appear in a JOIN clause instead of a comma?
recall.a: Yes — `JOIN json_each(e.payload, '$.items') AS i` is the same lateral join; it may reference earlier tables.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT NVL(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category, SUM(i.value:qty::INT) AS units FROM raw_order_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:items) i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = e.payload:order_id::INT JOIN products p ON p.product_id = i.value:product_id::INT WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1;

exercises.title: Revenue by tag without the items × tags fan-out
exercises.question: Marketing: how much gross revenue came from orders carrying each tag?
exercises.prompt: Return tag, tagged_orders (number of valid orders with that tag) and gross_revenue (sum over those orders of the JSON items' qty * price, rounded to 2 decimals). Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') in the orders table. Careful: flattening tags and items in the same FROM multiplies rows — compute each order's value first.
hints: If an order has 3 items and 2 tags, a double flatten gives 6 rows — each item counted twice.
Step 1 (CTE): one row per event with its order value. Step 2: flatten tags and join the CTE.

WITH order_value AS (SELECT e.event_id, SUM((i.value->>'$.qty')*(i.value->>'$.price')) AS order_value FROM raw_order_events e, json_each(e.payload,'$.items') i GROUP BY e.event_id) SELECT t.value AS tag, COUNT(*) AS tagged_orders, ROUND(SUM(v.order_value),2) ...
exercises.why: Double-flatten fan-out is the semi-structured version of the join fan-out from Module 2 — and it inflates revenue silently.

recall.q: Why aggregate items before flattening tags?
recall.a: Because items × tags is a cross product per event; aggregating first keeps one row per order.

exercises.snowflake: WITH order_value AS (SELECT e.event_id, SUM(i.value:qty::INT * i.value:price::NUMBER(10,2)) AS order_value FROM raw_order_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:items) i GROUP BY 1) SELECT t.value::STRING AS tag, COUNT(*) AS tagged_orders, ROUND(SUM(v.order_value), 2) AS gross_revenue FROM raw_order_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:tags) t JOIN order_value v ON v.event_id = e.event_id JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = e.payload:order_id::INT WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1;

exercises.title: Reconcile JSON lines with order_items
exercises.question: Finance sign-off: do the flattened JSON lines tie out to order_items, order by order?
exercises.prompt: Compare every event's order with order_items and return ONE row with: orders_compared (number of events, 60), orders_matching (events whose JSON line count, total qty and value ROUND(SUM(qty*price),2) all equal those of order_items for the same order_id — an order with no lines on both sides counts as matching), json_total_value and table_total_value (sum of all line values on each side, rounded to 2 decimals; all orders, no status filter).
hints: Aggregate each side to one row per order_id first (two CTEs), then join them.
Order 60 has an empty items array and no order_items rows: use LEFT JOINs and COALESCE(…, 0) so it compares 0 = 0.

WITH json_side AS (... LEFT JOIN json_each(e.payload,'$.items') i ON 1=1 GROUP BY order_id), table_side AS (... FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_compared, SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_matching, ...
exercises.why: Reconciliation queries (counts, sums, per-key matches) are how you earn trust in a new pipeline. Notice the JSON even reproduces the duplicate lines 149/150 — tying out proves consistency, not correctness.

recall.q: Why compare per order instead of only grand totals?
recall.a: Offsetting errors can make totals match while individual orders differ; per-key matching catches them.

exercises.snowflake: Same CTE structure with LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:items, OUTER => TRUE). In Snowflake you'd typically write the mismatch list with a FULL OUTER JOIN of the two aggregates and `WHERE j.value IS DISTINCT FROM t.value`.

exercises.title: Walk a whole document (RECURSIVE flatten)
exercises.question: Platform team: list every leaf value in event 4's payload with its full path, to document the schema.
exercises.prompt: Use json_tree on event 4's payload and return path (the fullkey column, e.g. $.customer.id) and leaf_value (the atom column) for every element that is NOT an object or array.
hints: json_tree walks every nested level (json_each only one level).
Its columns include fullkey (full path), type and atom (the scalar value).
SELECT t.fullkey AS path, t.atom AS leaf_value FROM raw_order_events e, json_tree(e.payload) t WHERE e.event_id = 4 AND t.type NOT IN ('object','array');
exercises.why: Recursive flattening is the fastest way to document an unfamiliar JSON source — or to diff two versions of a payload schema. (SQLite quotes some keys in fullkey, e.g. $."order_id" — that is still a valid path.)
exercises.snowflake: SELECT f.path, f.value AS leaf_value FROM raw_order_events e, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload, RECURSIVE => TRUE) f WHERE e.event_id = 4 AND TYPEOF(f.value) NOT IN ('OBJECT','ARRAY');

worked_example.question: Explode event 4's items and tags to see what json_each returns.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT 'item' AS array_name, i.key, i.value, i.type
FROM raw_order_events e, json_each(e.payload, '$.items') i
WHERE e.event_id = 4
UNION ALL
SELECT 'tag', t.key, t.value, t.type
FROM raw_order_events e, json_each(e.payload, '$.tags') t
WHERE e.event_id = 4;
worked_example.explanation: Each array element becomes a row: `key` is its position, `value` the element (a JSON object for items, a plain string for tags), `type` its JSON type. Snowflake's FLATTEN returns the same idea as columns SEQ, KEY, PATH, INDEX, VALUE, THIS.

recipe:
**Recipe: flatten an array in 4 moves**

1. **Put the table-valued function next to the table:** `FROM raw_order_events e, json_each(e.payload, '$.items') i`.
   For every event, `json_each` produces one row per array element (it can see `e` — that's what LATERAL means).
2. **Read the element:** `i.value ->> '$.qty'` for object elements, `i.value` for scalar elements (tags),
   `i.key` = 0-based position.
3. **Keep parents with no elements** when they matter: `LEFT JOIN json_each(e.payload, '$.tags') t ON 1 = 1`
   (Snowflake: `FLATTEN(..., OUTER => TRUE)`). An inner flatten silently drops events whose array is empty or missing.
4. **Never flatten two independent arrays in one FROM** unless you want the cross product (items × tags).
   Aggregate one array first (CTE), then join.

```sql
SELECT e.event_id,
       i.key                       AS line_no,
       i.value ->> '$.product_id'  AS product_id,
       i.value ->> '$.qty'         AS qty
FROM raw_order_events AS e,
     json_each(e.payload, '$.items') AS i;
```
snowflake_notes:
```sql
-- One row per item
SELECT e.event_id,
       e.payload:order_id::INT        AS order_id,
       i.index                        AS line_no,
       i.value:product_id::INT        AS product_id,
       i.value:qty::INT               AS qty,
       i.value:price::NUMBER(10,2)    AS price
FROM raw_order_events e,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:items) i;

-- Keep events without tags (OUTER => TRUE emits one row with NULL value)
SELECT e.event_id, t.value::STRING AS tag
FROM raw_order_events e,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:tags, OUTER => TRUE) t;

-- Walk the whole document (≈ json_tree)
SELECT f.path, f.key, f.value
FROM raw_order_events e,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload, RECURSIVE => TRUE) f
WHERE e.event_id = 4 AND TYPEOF(f.value) NOT IN ('OBJECT','ARRAY');
```

- FLATTEN output columns: `SEQ`, `KEY` (object key), `PATH`, `INDEX` (array position), `VALUE` (VARIANT), `THIS`.
- `LATERAL` is optional with FLATTEN (`, TABLE(FLATTEN(...))` works too) but makes intent explicit.
- **Pruning note:** FLATTEN runs on every row it's fed — filter the base table first (e.g. on `received_at`) so
  micro-partition pruning cuts the input before the explosion.
- Common production pattern: a staging view that flattens once (`stg_order_lines`), so every analyst doesn't
  re-implement FLATTEN with subtly different filters.
common_mistakes: Inner-flattening an optional array and losing the parent rows (forgetting OUTER => TRUE / LEFT JOIN … ON 1=1).
Flattening two arrays in one FROM and multiplying rows (items × tags).
Reading i.value as a number when it is an object — use i.value ->> '$.qty' (Snowflake i.value:qty::INT).
Counting COUNT(*) after a LEFT flatten — empty arrays still give 1 row; count COUNT(i.key) instead.
Flattening the whole raw table before filtering it — filter first, then explode.
recall: The right-hand table expression may reference columns of tables to its left, row by row.
SQLite equivalent of LATERAL FLATTEN(input => e.payload:items) i?
json_each(e.payload, '$.items') AS i in the FROM clause.
How do you keep events whose tags array is missing?
LEFT JOIN json_each(...) ON 1=1 / FLATTEN(..., OUTER => TRUE).
